prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as the sole prize part, credited to MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero. The reasoning is the one I would apply to any experiment. The Bistritzer-MacDonald calculation of 2011 predicted a specific, checkable thing, flat bands at a magic angle. Seven years later Jarillo-Herrero's group found correlated insulating and superconducting states at the predicted angle. That is the original decisive experiment for the claim the citation makes, and it has been reproduced in transport and in STM spectroscopy by many independent groups. The twist angle has become a control knob that opens a regime of electron physics that could not be reached before, which is the kind of door-opening I weigh most. Having re-read the round-1 exchange, the chair's questions did not change my mind, and I address them directly. On Andrei, the pre-2018 STM work reported Van Hove singularities and layer-decoupling or localisation signatures in twisted layers. As I understand the record it did not locate the magic angle, did not show a flat band at that angle, and did not show insulating or superconducting behaviour. It is a credible precursor strand, and I would want the citation worded so that it does not claim priority for the field as a whole. On the first authors of the 2018 papers and the hBN device work, the statutes force a choice, and the leadership of the experimental programme is clear, so I find the omission defensible if the committee records it openly. On maturity, the pairing mechanism is open, but the phenomenon is reproduced after about seven years, and earlier prizes have recognised observed phenomena before the mechanism was understood. A common standard I would apply to B033 and B026 is independent confirmation of the claimed result, not of the explanation. By that standard both pass.
statement.case_against: The weakest point remains the third seat and the narrowness of a three-name credit. Andrei's early STM evidence is real, the 2018 first authors and the Dean and Kim device work fall outside the limit, and the committee will be read as making a priority statement, so I cannot call the attribution closed, only the most defensible available. I also take seriously that device-to-device twist-angle disorder and strain mean the superconducting phase diagram varies between samples, and that the continuum model is an idealisation that relaxation modifies quantitatively. A committee that wants to be absolutely sure could reasonably say the field has not yet separated which features are generic from which are sample-specific. My answer is that the correlated insulator and superconducting phenomena are generic enough to be seen by many groups, but a clean verdict on the mechanism is not available and the citation must not imply one. Finally, 2010 already honoured graphene, and the committee must be satisfied that this is a distinct achievement. I think it is, because the object is an engineered moire structure and not the isolation of the material, but it is a fair challenge.

responses.point: The third seat should go to Bistritzer on the logic of the joint 2011 prediction, while Andrei's pre-2018 STM work remains an open uncertainty rather than a dismissed claim.
responses.response: I agree with this, and I am glad you moved to Bistritzer on the strength of the prediction-plus-discovery chain, because it is the structure I rely on too. On the chair's question I have worked through what Andrei's group could and could not show. Their STM measurements saw Van Hove singularities and a breakdown of layer decoupling at certain twist angles, which is an independent indication that twisted layers change the electronic structure. It did not identify the magic angle or the correlated and superconducting states, which are what the citation claims. I would therefore not give her a seat over Bistritzer, but I would ask that the committee record that her work was examined and described as a precursor. I would also ask you whether your concern about relaxation and strain would change the wording of the citation. My view is that it should not, as long as the citation says the flat bands were predicted and the correlated states were discovered, and says nothing about their microscopic origin.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are a clear invention verified in several laboratories, a strong fallback, but the pending redefinition of the second makes this year a less natural moment than for B033.
responses.response: I accept that the clock case is strong on exactly my criteria: a concrete invention, the magic-wavelength scheme, and independent intercomparisons at the 10^-18 level. I also think Lindroth is right that the redefinition of the second should not be cited as a reason for timing, and I would withdraw my own earlier reference to it as a maturity concern, since it is a decision about metrology and not a test of the physics. Where I still differ from you is on what the prize is asked to reward. B026 is an extraordinary improvement of an established measurement, with overlap against 2005 and 2012 that I think the committee can answer but that remains a real argument. B033 opens a new regime of physics. If the graphene credit proved intractable I would turn to B026 as my fallback, and I would be comfortable with the Katori and Ye credit. The question I put back to you is whether you would accept the same common standard for both: independent confirmation of the claimed result, with no requirement that the mechanism or the downstream applications be settled.

responses.point: The lattice clock solves a different problem from combs and single ions, with a clean two-name credit that fits the limit, and sample dependence in B033 makes it less settled than the clocks.
responses.response: Your distinction between the comb as a ruler, the single ion as controlled quantum system, and the lattice as a way to keep many-atom stability without perturbing the transition is persuasive, and I would not call B026 a mere refinement. On sample dependence I would hold B033 to the same test as the clocks, namely whether independent laboratories see the claimed effect with their own devices. For the clocks, comparisons across laboratories converge on one number. For twisted graphene, many groups with their own devices see the insulating and superconducting states, although the precise twist angles, critical temperatures and phase diagrams vary. The existence of the phenomena is confirmed, and the quantitative variation is a legitimate open point about the physics rather than a failure of verification. I therefore still prefer B033, and I would not stop you from placing B026 first if you are persuaded that a compact two-name credit is the safer path. I would only ask that we compare what each prize is a discovery of.

responses.point: Magic-angle graphene is timely but somewhat early because the superconducting mechanism is unresolved, and the chair asks for a distinction from earlier prizes given before mechanisms were understood.
responses.response: I take the chair's distinction seriously and have tried to answer it from the record. Earlier prizes recognised the observed phenomenon, such as the quantum Hall effects and high-temperature superconductivity, while the mechanism was still debated. What matters under our rule is whether the original experiment is identified and verified, and for magic-angle graphene it is. The reservation that I think deserves more weight is the one you identified earlier, sample dependence, because it bears on how the phenomenon is described. I would suggest two safeguards in the citation: it should say prediction and discovery of the states and avoid any statement on pairing, and it should not suggest that the whole moire field began in 2018. If the committee cannot accept that wording, I would be willing to discuss waiting, but I do not find the open mechanism sufficient on its own to postpone.

responses.point: The decisive chain is prediction followed by discovery of the correlated phases, and the citation should not read as a statement of priority that implies the field began in 2018.
responses.response: I agree about the citation and I think your caution is the right one for the statement the committee would make. In round 1 I asked that Andrei's chronology be examined, and having examined what her pre-2018 STM work did and did not show, I accept your framing that the prediction and the 2018 discovery form the core, provided the record states plainly that earlier twisted-layer spectroscopy and device work exist. I would resist, however, moving too far from the word precursor to secondary, since I do not want our deliberations to suggest that the earlier experiments were not valuable. Our wording to the Academy should be careful and narrow.

uncertainties: Exact scope and dating of Andrei's pre-2018 STM and transport results, which I am relying on from my own recollection rather than from a checked record, and whether any part of it should alter the citation.
Whether device-to-device twist-angle disorder, strain and lattice relaxation make the superconducting phase diagram too sample-dependent for the committee to be absolutely sure of the claim.
Whether crediting the group leader and not the first authors of the 2018 experimental papers will be accepted as defensible under the three-person limit.
Whether a committee member who values the compact B026 credit would find the graphene credit settled enough, and how the fallback ordering of B026 versus B009 should be set if B033 fails.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name on the shortlist. My field of electron microscopy is adjacent to the moire and clock topics but I have no collaboration with MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero, Andrei, Katori, Ye or the topological-insulator candidates. I share a first name with Eva Andrei and nothing else. Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague and no shortlisted candidate is connected to either of us. I see no need for recusal.
